title: Daily habits: stock, customers, records and profit
course_title: Introduction to Small Business and Trading

say: Daily habits: stock, customers, records and profit.
This is the video for module three of Introduction to Small Business and Trading.
Once you are open, profit is won or lost in daily habits. For a trader, stock is money sitting on a shelf. Every carton that does not sell is cash you cannot use.

say: The habit that most often decides whether a small business survives is simple: keep business money and personal money apart.

say: Once a week, on the same day, count every item and multiply by its cost price. That total is your stock value at cost, and it shows up losses from theft, spoilage or mistakes early.

say: When new stock arrives, put it behind the old, so older items sell first. This is called first in, first out.

say: Check expiry dates when you buy, and refuse goods close to expiry unless you know you can sell them in time.

say: Keep food off the floor, away from damp, sun and rats. Store kerosene, insecticides and detergents separately from food.

say: Patience in Benin City found one brand of cooking oil had sat for over a month. She stopped reordering it and put that money into faster items.
And never sell expired or damaged goods. It can harm customers and destroys trust.

say: Be honest about quality, and count change in front of the customer. When Mercy in Jos sold a dented tin of milk, she listened, apologised, replaced it at once, and now checks every tin when stock arrives.
Give credit only to regulars, with a limit, for example 3,000 naira, a date, and a written credit page.

panel.heading: Service and credit
left: Credit only to regulars, written down
right: New credit before old is paid

say: Unpaid credit is one of the most common reasons small businesses collapse. Money owed to you cannot restock your table. So give no new credit until the old balance is paid.

left: Credit only to regulars, written down
right: New credit before old is paid

say: Step one. Keep business money in its own place: a separate purse or box at first, and later a separate bank or mobile money account.

panel.heading: Separate the money
items: A separate purse, box or account for the business
Pay yourself a fixed amount from profit
Write down anything else you take
Never pay home costs straight from the stall

say: Step two. Pay yourself a fixed amount from profit, on the same day each week.

panel.heading: Separate the money
items: A separate purse, box or account for the business
Pay yourself a fixed amount from profit
Write down anything else you take
Never pay home costs straight from the stall

say: Step three. Record anything else you take as owner drawings, including goods taken home.

panel.heading: Separate the money
items: A separate purse, box or account for the business
Pay yourself a fixed amount from profit
Write down anything else you take
Never pay home costs straight from the stall

say: Step four. Never pay school fees or food straight from the stall's cash. Each day, write sales, stock bought, other costs and what you took. Then count your cash. It should match your book.

panel.rule: Pay yourself first, then pay personal costs from your own money.

say: Here is a worked example. Joy's sales for June are 380,000 naira.
Cost of goods sold is opening stock, plus purchases, minus closing stock. For Joy that is 70,000 plus 300,000 minus 75,000, which is 295,000 naira.

card.title: Joy's profit for June
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: So her gross profit is 380,000 minus 295,000, which is 85,000 naira.

card.title: Joy's profit for June
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: Now her running costs. Transport 12,000, levies 3,000, bags 4,000 and phone data 3,000 naira.

card.title: Joy's profit for June
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: That is 22,000 naira. So her net profit is 85,000 minus 22,000, which is 63,000 naira.
She paid herself 40,000, so 23,000 stays in the business to grow it. Without the book, she would only have guessed.

say: A profitable business can still run out of cash, if money is tied up in stock or credit, or a big purchase falls in the same week as rent. So look ahead each month.

say: Write goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. That is called SMART.

say: Lami in Kano wants 90,000 naira net profit a month. She works backwards and finds she needs about 22,100 naira of sales a day. Now she knows her target.

say: At the end of each month, spend one hour with your book. A month below target is information, not failure. Find the cause, and change one thing.

say: To remember. Count stock weekly and sell the oldest first. Give credit only with limits, dates and records. Keep business money apart and pay yourself a fixed amount. Record every sale, cost and drawing. And review your numbers every month.

Record every sale, cost and drawing
Review every month

say: Now start the habits. Count your stock twice, a week apart. Open a credit page and a regular customer list. Keep your record book for seven days, and write three SMART goals.
Then continue with the lessons below.
